hero.text: The one board that splits its papers by century rather than by skill. Twentieth-century literature on one paper, nineteenth and twenty-first century non-fiction on the other.

blocks.title: Where these figures come from
text: Component titles, durations and weightings were read from the **Summary of Assessment** table in the WJEC Eduqas GCSE English Language specification. The reading and writing weightings come from the **Assessment Objectives and Weightings** section of the same document.
Eduqas materials are **linked, never copied**. No question, source text or mark scheme wording is reproduced here, and no paper-sharing site is linked.
**RCF English is not affiliated with, endorsed by or approved by Eduqas or WJEC.**

Eduqas divides English Language differently from the other three boards. AQA, Edexcel and OCR all split their papers broadly by **kind of text** - fiction on one paper, non-fiction on the other. Eduqas splits by **century**.

Component 1 is twentieth-century literature and your own creative prose. Component 2 puts a nineteenth-century non-fiction text beside a twenty-first-century one and asks for transactional or persuasive writing. If you have prepared for another board, this is the difference that will catch you out.

blocks.heading: The qualification at a glance
rows: 20th Century Literature Reading and Creative Prose Writing. Written examination, **1 hour 45 minutes**, **40% of the qualification**.
19th and 21st Century Non-Fiction Reading and Transactional/Persuasive Writing. Written examination, **2 hours**, **60% of the qualification**.
Eduqas states that SPaG makes up **20%** of the qualification.
Eduqas describes its **long tariff questions as worth 10 marks**.
None. Both components use unseen material.

blocks.title: Three things the structure tells you to do
text: **Component 2 is worth half as much again as Component 1** - 60% against 40% - and it is the longer paper at two hours. If revision time has to be divided unevenly, this is the paper that should get more of it.

**Reading and writing are worth the same.** Writing is 50% of the qualification across the two papers. Candidates who treat the writing task as the thing they do after the reading are gambling with half their grade.

**Spelling, punctuation and grammar are 20% on their own.** That is a fifth of the whole qualification, it needs no wider reading, and it is the most improvable part of the course. Five minutes of checking at the end of each paper protects more marks here than anywhere else.

blocks.heading: Assessment objectives
blocks.caption: From the specification's Assessment Objectives and Weightings section. Eduqas groups them under reading and writing rather than listing per-component percentages on the summary table.
rows: Reading and understanding a range of texts: identifying and interpreting information and ideas, explaining and analysing how writers use language and structure, comparing writers' ideas and perspectives, and evaluating texts critically with textual reference.

Communicating clearly, effectively and imaginatively, adapting tone, style and register for form, purpose and audience; organising information and ideas; and using a range of vocabulary and sentence structures with accurate spelling and punctuation.
Assessed and reported separately. It does not contribute to the overall GCSE grade.

blocks.heading: The spoken language endorsement
text: Component 3 is non-exam assessment and is **unweighted**. Eduqas states plainly that speaking skills are assessed but do not contribute to the overall grade.
bullets: It is a **compulsory part of the course** even though it earns no marks towards the grade.
It is **reported separately** on the certificate.
The arrangements for spoken language are **consistent across all examination boards**, so guidance written for AQA, Edexcel or OCR applies here too.
Eduqas publishes guidance for candidates with communication or hearing needs as an appendix to the specification.

blocks.heading: Common questions about Eduqas English Language

items.q: What is the difference between Eduqas and WJEC?
a: They are the same organisation. WJEC is the awarding body; **Eduqas** is the brand it uses for qualifications designed for England, which follow the English reformed GCSE rules.
Documents are often headed *WJEC Eduqas*, which is why both names appear on the specification. If you are entered for C700QS you are taking the Eduqas qualification.
**Component 2.** It pairs a nineteenth-century non-fiction text with a twenty-first-century one.

This is worth noting if you have prepared using another board's material. AQA puts its nineteenth-century source on Paper 2 as well, but pairs it with a modern non-fiction text; Edexcel and OCR both put their nineteenth-century text on the *fiction* paper. Eduqas is the only one of the four whose papers are divided by century rather than by text type.

items.q: Are there set texts to learn?
a: No. Both components use unseen material, so there is nothing to memorise and no prescribed reading list.
This means revision is entirely about method: how to approach an unfamiliar text under time pressure, and how to plan a piece of writing quickly.

items.q: How much does spelling and punctuation actually matter?
a: A great deal. Eduqas states that spelling, punctuation and grammar make up **20%** of the qualification.
That is a fifth of the grade available for something that requires no reading, no set text and no wider knowledge - only care. It is the single most improvable part of the course.

items.q: Can I use AQA or OCR past papers to practise?
a: For reading and writing skills, yes. All four boards assess the same national assessment objectives, so analysis of language and structure, comparison and evaluation all transfer.

For timing and structure, no. The component split, durations and weightings differ, and Eduqas's division by century means the text pairings are unlike any other board's. Use other boards' material for skills practice and Eduqas's own papers for full mock conditions.

pages.title: Eduqas Component 1: 20th Century Literature and Creative Prose
pages.metaTitle: Eduqas GCSE English Language Component 1: Structure and Method | RCF English
pages.description: Eduqas GCSE English Language Component 1 explained: a 20th century literature extract, the reading questions, and the creative prose writing task. 1 hour 45 minutes, 40%.
pages.keywords: Eduqas component 1, 20th century literature reading, Eduqas creative prose writing, C700QS component 1

hero.text: One unseen twentieth-century prose extract, a set of reading questions, and a piece of creative prose of your own. One hour and forty-five minutes.

blocks.title: Where these figures come from
text: Duration and weighting read from the Summary of Assessment table in the Eduqas specification. Eduqas materials are linked, never copied. RCF English is not affiliated with, endorsed by or approved by Eduqas or WJEC.

**Per-question mark allocations are not stated here**, because they were not verified from the specification. Use the [past papers](global-english/gcse/eduqas/papers/) for the exact marks on each question.

blocks.heading: Component 1 at a glance
rows: 20th Century Literature Reading and Creative Prose Writing
One unseen prose extract from the twentieth century, with a series of questions
One piece of creative prose writing, from a choice

blocks.heading: The reading section
text: The extract is twentieth-century prose, and it is unseen. The questions move through the extract, generally from straightforward retrieval towards analysis and evaluation, which means the paper gets harder as it goes on rather than starting hard.
bullets: **Early questions are usually short and factual.** Answer them in a phrase or a sentence and move on. Spending three minutes on a low-tariff question is the commonest way to run short of time later.
**Middle questions ask about language and structure.** Quote briefly, say what the choice does to the reader, then take it one step further. Naming a technique earns nothing on its own.

**The long questions are worth 10 marks.** Eduqas calls these its *long tariff* questions. They need developed paragraphs, not a list of points, and the mark is as much for how the answer is built as for what it contains.

**Evaluation questions ask what you think, with evidence.** A statement is offered and you agree, disagree or qualify it - supported by close reference. An answer that describes the extract without judging it cannot reach the top band.

**Structure is half of the language-and-structure question**, and it is the half most candidates ignore. Where does the focus shift? What is withheld, and until when? Why does the extract end where it does?

blocks.heading: The creative prose writing section
text: You produce one piece of creative prose from a choice. Since reading and writing are each worth 50% of the qualification, this section carries real weight - it is not an afterthought at the end of a reading paper.
bullets: **Choose the title you can finish**, not the one that sounds most interesting. A controlled description of a single scene will outscore an ambitious three-part story that collapses in the second part.
**Narrow the scope hard.** Most high-scoring creative writing at GCSE covers minutes rather than years, and one place rather than several.
**Decide the ending before you start.** An ending that merely stops is the commonest way to lose marks in the top band, and it is entirely avoidable.

**Protect the technical accuracy marks.** Spelling, punctuation and grammar are 20% of the whole qualification. Vary sentence length deliberately, check the punctuation of any dialogue, and leave five minutes at the end.
**Plan for about 45 minutes of writing** including planning and checking, and keep to it. Running over here cannot be recovered, because the reading marks are already spent.

blocks.title: A timing plan for Component 1
text: **0-10 min** read the extract once for what happens and who is telling it, then read the questions.
**10-60 min** the reading questions, weighted by their marks. Short questions get minutes; the 10-mark questions get the bulk.
**60-100 min** the creative writing, including five minutes planning at the start.
**100-105 min** check the writing only - sentence endings, paragraph breaks, spelling. Do not return to the reading section; those marks are already made.

pages.metaTitle: Eduqas GCSE English Language Component 2: Structure and Method | RCF English
pages.description: Eduqas GCSE English Language Component 2 explained: 19th and 21st century non-fiction reading and transactional or persuasive writing. 2 hours, 60% of the qualification.
pages.keywords: Eduqas component 2, 19th and 21st century non-fiction, Eduqas transactional writing, persuasive writing Eduqas

hero.text: Two non-fiction texts written roughly two hundred years apart, and two pieces of transactional writing. Two hours, and sixty per cent of the qualification.

blocks.title: Where these figures come from
text: Duration and weighting read from the Summary of Assessment table in the Eduqas specification. The **per-question mark allocations below** come from Eduqas's own [Component 2 additional assessment materials](https://www.eduqas.co.uk/media/fkopbmoc/5-component-2-additional-assessment-materials.pdf), which prints each question with its tariff in brackets, and whose front cover states the two section totals and the timing for the writing section. Eduqas materials are linked, never copied. RCF English is not affiliated with, endorsed by or approved by Eduqas or WJEC.

**One figure below is not Eduqas's.** The 20 marks shown against each of the two writing tasks is not stated in that document. Eduqas gives Section B as 40 marks and advises 30 minutes on each of the two questions; splitting it evenly is an inference, and it is marked as one. Check a [past paper](global-english/gcse/eduqas/papers/) before relying on it.

blocks.heading: Component 2 at a glance
rows: 19th and 21st Century Non-Fiction Reading and Transactional/Persuasive Writing
**60% of the qualification** - the larger of the two papers
Unseen non-fiction: one nineteenth-century text and one twenty-first-century text

blocks.title: The century gap is the point of this paper
text: Pairing a nineteenth-century text with a twenty-first-century one is not decoration. It is what makes comparison possible: two writers on a related subject, separated by two centuries of changed assumptions about class, gender, science, empire and what may be said in public.

**The nineteenth-century text is the one to prepare for.** Its sentences are longer, its vocabulary is less familiar, and its tone is often formal in a way that can read as cold or pompous to a modern ear when it is neither. Reading a few nineteenth-century letters, speeches, travel accounts or newspaper columns before the examination is the single most useful preparation for this paper.

**Do not mistake unfamiliarity for difficulty of thought.** A Victorian writer arguing for better drains is making a plain argument in an ornate register. Translate the register in your head and the argument is usually straightforward.

blocks.heading: Where the 80 marks sit
blocks.caption: The reading tariffs are the shape Eduqas prints in its own Component 2 assessment materials. The 20 marks against each writing task is an inference from two equally timed tasks sharing 40 marks, not a published figure.
rows: Retrieval from the first text. One fact each, written plainly.
How the writer shows something about the first text. The question names *what he says* and *language, tone and structure*, and both halves must be answered.
**Evaluation.** *How well* does the text convey the writer's feelings? Not what the feelings are, but how successfully they are conveyed.
Short synthesis across **both** texts. Information, not analysis - there are no marks for method here.
Comparison across **both** texts: the subject itself, and how each writer gets their feelings across.
Two transactional or persuasive tasks, about 30 minutes each: five minutes planning, twenty-five writing.

blocks.title: The two questions students most often misread
text: **A4 is an evaluation question, not a feelings question.** The marks are in the words *how well*. An answer that lists what the writer feels, however accurately, has answered only the first of the two bullets.
**A5 is worth four marks and wants facts.** Analysing language here earns nothing, and it costs the time A6 needs. Five minutes is enough.

blocks.heading: The reading section
bullets: **Read one text and answer its questions before moving to the second.** Reading both first and then starting is slower and leads to confusing the two.
**Short questions want short answers.** Give the number of points the marks ask for and stop.
**Language questions want effect, not labels.** Say what a word or image does to the reader, and use terminology only where it helps you say it.
**The comparison question is where the paper is won or lost.** Both writers must appear in every paragraph, and each paragraph should say how the two differ - not describe one and then the other.
**Attitude and viewpoint matter more than subject.** The question is usually about how each writer feels about the subject and how you can tell, rather than what the subject is.

blocks.heading: Transactional and persuasive writing
text: The writing section asks for transactional or persuasive pieces - writing that does a job for a stated reader: a letter, an article, a speech, a report, a review, a leaflet.
bullets: **Obey the form, audience and purpose.** They are stated, not implied. A letter to a head teacher and an article for a local newspaper are different registers, and adapting register is explicitly credited.
**Open in the register, not with a run-up.** The first sentence should already sound like the form you have been asked for.
**Structure by argument, not by paragraph count.** Two developed points beat four thin ones, and a concession you then answer is worth more than another point.
**Do not draw the layout.** Time spent on boxes, columns and headings is time not spent on the writing that is actually marked.
**Protect the 20% for spelling, punctuation and grammar.** Leave five minutes at the end of each piece.

blocks.title: A timing plan for Component 2
text: **0-10 min** read the first text and its questions.
**10-40 min** answer on the first text.
**40-70 min** read and answer on the second text.
**70-85 min** the comparison question, which needs both texts and a plan.
**85-115 min** the writing section, including planning.
**115-120 min** check the writing. This paper is 60% of the qualification, so the last five minutes are worth more here than on Component 1.

blocks.title: The annotated exemplars are the most useful thing on this list
text: Eduqas publishes real candidate answers with examiner annotation and the mark awarded. They show exactly why one answer scored what it did on the same question another answer failed.

Almost no student reads them. Working through the Component 2 exemplars once will teach you more about the standard than doing a third past paper will, because a past paper tells you what you got wrong while an exemplar tells you what right looks like.

blocks.title: The other boards
text: All four boards now have at least one RCF model paper: the [AQA Paper 2 model paper](global-english/gcse/aqa/papers/rcf-model-paper-2/), the [Edexcel model papers](global-english/gcse/edexcel/papers/) and the [OCR Component 01 model paper](global-english/gcse/ocr/papers/rcf-model-component-1/).

The AQA Paper 2 model paper is also useful practice for Eduqas Component 2, since both pair a nineteenth-century non-fiction text with a modern one and both end in a comparison. The question tariffs differ, so use it for the reading skills rather than for the timing.

items.q: Where can I get Eduqas past papers free?
a: From Eduqas itself. The [past papers and mark schemes portal](https://www.eduqas.co.uk/home/past-papers-and-mark-schemes/) carries question papers and mark schemes for past series, and the specification and sample materials are free to download.
Some recent series are restricted to registered centres for a period after the examination. Your school will have access; ask a teacher rather than looking for the paper on a sharing site.

items.q: Should I use WJEC papers as well?
a: Be careful. WJEC and Eduqas are the same organisation, but the WJEC-branded GCSE English Language is the Welsh qualification and its structure is not identical to C700QS.
For mock conditions use papers headed **Eduqas** and carrying C700QS. WJEC papers are useful extra reading practice but will mislead you on timing.

items.q: How many past papers should I do?
a: Fewer than most students think, and each one properly. Two papers done under timed conditions and then marked carefully against the mark scheme are worth more than six attempted and never marked.
Read one set of annotated exemplars before your second paper. Knowing what the examiner rewards changes how you write the next one.
